title: FGM: the mandatory reporting duty for under-18s
blurb: Know exactly when the s5B FGM duty applies, how and when to report to police, and when ordinary safeguarding applies instead.
question: Amina, 15, attends a sexual health clinic with painful periods. She tells the nurse she was 'cut' as a small child before coming to the UK. What must the nurse do, by when, and can she ask the safeguarding lead to report it for her?

teach.body: Section 5B of the Female Genital Mutilation Act 2003 (inserted by the Serious Crime Act 2015, in force 31 October 2015) requires regulated health and social care professionals and teachers in England and Wales to notify the police when, in the course of their work, they discover that FGM appears to have been carried out on a girl under 18. In plain English: if a girl tells you, or you see signs, you report it to the police yourself.

rows.label: How
values: The girl tells you, in any words

rows.label: Example
values: 'I was cut when I was little'

rows.label: Proviso
values: Must be from the girl herself
No reason to think it was necessary surgery

teach.caption: Do not carry out a genital examination to look for FGM unless it is already part of the care you are giving.

children.edge: Girl under 18 discloses, or signs seen
children.label: Duty applies: report to police

children.edge: Woman 18+ (even if cut as a child)
children.label: Support; assess risk to others

teach.caption: The relevant age is her age when you discover it, not when FGM was done.

head: Rule
Detail
rows: Police for the area where the girl lives; call 101
Best practice by close of the next working day
Orally or in writing; identify the girl and explain why
The police reference number, in the notes
teach.caption: A longer timeframe is for exceptional cases where a report may itself put the child at immediate risk: consult colleagues and record decisions.

teach.body: The professional who discovers the case must make the report: it cannot be handed to a safeguarding lead to do instead. The one exception is where you know another person in your profession has already reported the same act; for this purpose all regulated healthcare professionals count as one profession (s5B(6)). If records are unclear, report and say a report may already exist. Reporting does not breach confidentiality (s5B(7)).
teach.cite: FGM Act 2003 s5B(6)-(7); Home Office procedural information

teach.body: Amina is under 18 and has told the nurse herself, in her own words ('cut'), so the duty applies. The nurse reports personally to the police by calling 101, ideally by the close of the next working day and certainly within one month, and records the reference number. She also informs the safeguarding lead and follows local safeguarding procedures, including thinking about younger sisters. She explains to Amina, sensitively, what will happen, and arranges her clinical care.

teach.text: Known vs at risk: the mandatory police report is for known cases (disclosed by the girl or seen). A girl at risk, a disclosure by a parent, or a woman aged 18 or over all go through normal safeguarding procedures instead. Genital piercing in an under-18 is also reported under the duty.

items: s5B: regulated professionals report FGM in a girl under 18 to police, discovered at work by her disclosure or by visible signs.
Call 101; best practice by close of the next working day; legal maximum one month.
Personal duty: cannot be delegated to a safeguarding lead; no need to repeat if another healthcare professional already reported.
At risk, parent disclosure or women 18+: normal safeguarding, not the mandatory duty.
Make a safeguarding referral as well; 999 if immediate danger.

summary: You can now decide when the FGM mandatory reporting duty applies, report it personally to the police within the right timescale, and explain why it cannot be delegated. You can also route at-risk cases, parental disclosures and adult women through normal safeguarding.

A.q: A school nurse in England learns on Monday afternoon, through a disclosure by a 14-year-old girl, that she has had FGM. There is no immediate danger. By when should the police report ideally be made?
options: By the close of the next working day
Within one month, as the law allows
Within 72 hours of the disclosure
At the next multi-agency safeguarding meeting
A.why: The procedural information says best practice is to report by the close of the next working day. One month is the legal maximum for exceptional cases.

whyNot.1: One month is the legal maximum, not the expected timescale.
whyNot.2: 72 hours is not the FGM reporting standard.
whyNot.3: Waiting for a meeting delays the personal duty.

A.q: During her daughter's asthma review, Mrs Diallo tells the practice nurse that her 12-year-old daughter Fatou had FGM as a baby. Fatou is not present. What should the nurse do?
options: Report to the police under the mandatory duty
Follow local procedures and refer to social care
Wait until Fatou herself confirms the FGM at a visit
Record it and take no further action
A.why: The mandatory duty applies to disclosure by the girl herself. A parent's disclosure is handled through wider safeguarding, which in England is likely to include a social care referral.

whyNot.0: The mandatory police report is not triggered by a parent's disclosure.
whyNot.2: Waiting leaves the safeguarding concern unaddressed.
whyNot.3: A disclosure of FGM in a child needs a safeguarding response.

A.q: Who must make the police report when a nurse discovers FGM in a 13-year-old?
options: The trust's named nurse for safeguarding
The consultant responsible for the girl
The nurse who made the discovery
The girl's parent, supported by the nurse
A.why: The duty is personal to the professional who discovers the case and cannot be transferred.

whyNot.0: The safeguarding lead can advise but cannot report in the nurse's place.
whyNot.1: The consultant has no duty unless they also discovered it.
whyNot.3: The duty falls on the professional, not the family.

B.q: Sara, 19, discloses at a gynaecology clinic that she had FGM aged 8. She has a 6-year-old sister at home. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Report to the police under the mandatory duty
Take no action, as Sara is now an adult
Refer her sister if Sara agrees to the referral
Support Sara and assess her sister's risk
B.why: The duty does not apply to women aged 18 or over at disclosure. Sara is supported, and the risk to her younger sister is assessed under local safeguarding procedures.

whyNot.0: The relevant age is at disclosure; Sara is 19.
whyNot.1: Her sister may be at risk, which needs a safeguarding response.
whyNot.2: Safeguarding her sister does not depend on Sara's agreement.

B.q: A children's nurse inserting a urinary catheter for Maryam, 9, after surgery notices genital appearances she believes show FGM. There is no record of any medical procedure. What should she do?
options: Arrange a specialist examination to confirm it first
Report to the police, as signs appear to show FGM
Ask Maryam's mother for an explanation first
Record her findings and refer to the GP
B.why: The duty applies when physical signs appear to show FGM and there is no reason to think it was necessary surgery. No clinical diagnosis is needed first.

whyNot.0: Confirmation is not required before reporting.
whyNot.2: Asking the family first may increase risk and is not required.
whyNot.3: A GP referral does not meet the duty to report to police.

B.q: A ward nurse finds that a doctor reported a 16-year-old's FGM to police last week. Must the nurse make a second report?
options: Yes, as each professional who discovers it must report individually
Yes, unless the girl has since turned 17
No, as healthcare professionals count as one profession
No, as the duty is the safeguarding lead's
B.why: s5B(6): the duty does not apply if another person in the same regulated profession has reported, and all regulated healthcare professionals count as one profession.

whyNot.0: A second report by another healthcare professional is not required.
whyNot.1: Her age is still under 18; the exception rests on the earlier report.
whyNot.3: The duty is personal, not the safeguarding lead's.

C.q: During a sexual health appointment, the nurse notices that Chloe, 16, has a genital piercing. Chloe says it was done at a piercing studio. Under the procedural information, what should the nurse do?
options: Make a report under the FGM mandatory duty
Record it, as it is cosmetic and lawful at 16
Refer to social care, as it is a suspected case
Advise Chloe about aftercare and infection signs
C.why: The procedural information advises that genital piercing in a girl under 18 should be reported under the duty.

whyNot.1: Genital piercing in an under-18 falls within the reporting guidance.
whyNot.2: It is a known case to report under the duty, not a suspected one.
whyNot.3: Aftercare advice does not discharge the reporting duty.

C.q: A health visitor learns that Halima, 6, is going on a 'long holiday' to a country with high FGM prevalence. Her older sister had FGM. What should the health visitor do?
options: Report to the police under the mandatory duty
Advise the family that FGM is illegal and wait for the holiday
Make a safeguarding referral, as Halima is at risk
Examine Halima to check whether FGM has occurred
C.why: The mandatory duty applies to known cases. A girl at risk is referred through local safeguarding procedures urgently.

whyNot.0: At-risk cases are not covered by the mandatory duty.
whyNot.1: Advice alone does not protect Halima.
whyNot.3: Examinations should not be carried out to look for FGM.

C.q: A nurse discovers FGM in a 14-year-old and is concerned that reporting today may lead the family to take the girl abroad tonight. What is the best course?
options: Delay reporting for the full legal month so that safety can be planned
Take no action until the family's travel is confirmed
Ask the girl's mother whether travel is planned
Consult the safeguarding lead; call 999 if danger is immediate
C.why: Where there is risk of serious immediate harm, professionals should report immediately to police, including dialling 999, and consult the safeguarding lead and record decisions.

whyNot.0: Delay increases the risk of her being taken abroad.
whyNot.1: Waiting for confirmation leaves her unprotected.
whyNot.2: Alerting the family may precipitate the harm.

reteach.title: Known, under 18, at work
reteach.question: How do I know quickly whether to call 101?

blocks.body: Gate 1: is she under 18 now? Gate 2: did she tell you herself, or did you see signs, in the course of your work? Gate 3: is there no reason to think it was a necessary medical procedure? If all three open, you personally call 101, ideally by the close of the next working day. If any is shut (adult, parent's disclosure, at risk only), use normal safeguarding procedures.

blocks.text: You cannot hand the report to the safeguarding lead. Reporting does not breach confidentiality.

explain.body: Regulated health and social care professionals and teachers in England and Wales, discovering FGM in a girl under 18 in the course of their work.

test.q: A nurse volunteering at a youth club is told by a 15-year-old that she has had FGM. Does the mandatory duty apply?
options: Yes, as she is a registered nurse
Yes, as the girl is under 18
No, as it was not in her professional work
No, as youth clubs are exempt from safeguarding
test.why: The duty applies to cases discovered in the course of professional work, not volunteering. She must still follow safeguarding procedures.

whyNot.0: Registration alone does not trigger the duty outside professional work.
whyNot.1: Age is one condition; the setting is the other.
whyNot.3: Safeguarding still applies; it is the mandatory duty that does not.

explain.body: The girl tells you (any words), or you observe physical signs with no reason to think it was necessary surgery. No full diagnosis is needed.

test.q: Which situation triggers the mandatory duty?
options: A girl, 11, tells the nurse she was 'cut'
An aunt says her niece, 9, had FGM
A woman, 20, says she had FGM aged 5
A girl, 8, is due to travel to a high-risk country
test.why: Disclosure by the girl herself, in any words, triggers the duty.

whyNot.1: Disclosure by a relative is handled through safeguarding.

explain.body: To the police for the girl's area, usually by calling 101; identify her and explain why; best practice next working day; maximum one month; record the reference number.

test.q: What is the legal maximum time for an FGM notification after discovery?
options: Two weeks
Five working days
Three months
One month
test.why: s5B(5)(c): before the end of one month from first discovery.

whyNot.0: Two weeks is not the statutory limit.
whyNot.1: Five working days is not the statutory limit.

explain.body: The duty cannot be transferred. It does not apply if another healthcare professional has already reported the same act. Reporting does not breach confidentiality.

test.q: A girl of 15 asks the nurse not to tell anyone about her FGM. How does this affect the duty?
options: The duty is waived at her request
The report must still be made
The report needs her written consent
The duty passes to her GP instead
test.why: The duty is mandatory and the disclosure does not breach confidentiality; the nurse explains sensitively why she must report.

whyNot.0: The girl cannot waive a statutory duty.
whyNot.3: The duty stays with the professional who discovered it.
